title: The Dark Side: Problems and Controversies
summary: Smartphones are amazing, but they also cause real problems. Some apps are designed to keep us scrolling, phones can distract drivers and walkers, and scammers try to trick us. Inside every phone are metals dug from mines far away, and old phones pile up as waste. But people are working hard on fixes, from phone-free classrooms to phones you can repair yourself!

sections.heading: Built to Keep You Scrolling
paragraphs: Have you ever picked up a phone to check one quick thing, and then looked up to discover that half an hour had vanished? If so, you are not alone, and it is not simply because you lack willpower. Many of the most popular apps are carefully designed to hold on to your attention for as long as possible.

To understand why, follow the money. Most social media apps, video sites and many games are free to download. The companies that make them still need to earn billions of dollars to pay their engineers, run their giant data centers and make a profit. A large part of that money comes from advertising. Advertisers pay to show their ads to people, so the more time people spend in an app, the more ads they see, and the more the company earns. Your attention, in other words, is the product being sold. People who study this call it the attention economy.

App designers have discovered many tricks that make it hard to stop. One is the endless feed, often called infinite scroll. On an old-fashioned website, you reached the bottom of a page and had to decide whether to click to the next one. That little pause was a natural stopping point. An endless feed removes the bottom of the page completely: new posts keep appearing as you swipe, so there is never a moment that says you are done. Video apps do something similar with autoplay, starting the next video automatically before you have decided whether you even want it.

Another trick is the unpredictable reward. Psychologists discovered decades ago, in experiments with animals, that a reward that arrives only sometimes, at random, keeps an animal pressing a lever more eagerly than a reward that comes every time. Slot machines in casinos work on the same principle. Pulling down a feed to refresh it is a bit like pulling the lever: sometimes you get an exciting new message or a funny video, sometimes nothing much. Because you never know, you keep checking.

Then there are notifications, the buzzes, banners and red dots that pull you back into apps throughout the day. Likes and hearts give a quick feeling of approval from friends. Streaks, which reward you for using an app every single day, make people worry about breaking the chain. None of these features is evil on its own, and some are genuinely useful. Together, though, they can make it very hard to put a phone down.

Sleep is one of the first things to suffer. Many young people keep phones in their bedrooms and use them late at night. Messages and games keep the brain excited when it should be winding down, and notifications can wake people up during the night. Bright screens close to the eyes may also make it a little harder to feel sleepy, although scientists think the excitement of what is on the screen probably matters more than the light itself. Sleep experts commonly recommend putting screens away an hour or so before bed and charging phones outside the bedroom.

The good news is that phones now include tools to fight back. Most have screen-time reports that show how many hours you spend in each app, timers that lock an app after a daily limit, do-not-disturb and bedtime modes that silence notifications, and settings that turn off autoplay. Some people even switch their screens to grayscale, removing the bright colors that make apps look so tempting. A little planning can make the phone work for you, instead of the other way around.

sections.heading: What Do Scientists Really Know?
paragraphs: Here is one of the biggest debates in science today: are smartphones and social media harming young people's mental health? It is a question that worries parents, teachers, doctors and governments, and the honest answer is that scientists do not yet fully agree.

Some facts are not in dispute. In the United States, Britain and several other countries, surveys show that rates of anxiety and depression among teenagers, especially girls, rose noticeably during the 2010s. That is the same decade in which smartphones and social media became an everyday part of teenage life. Psychologist Jean Twenge was one of the first researchers to point out this timing. In 2024, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt published a best-selling book called The Anxious Generation. He argued that a phone-based childhood, combined with less free play and independence in the real world, has caused a large rise in mental illness among young people. He pointed to four main harms: less time with friends in person, lost sleep, broken-up attention and something like addiction. He recommended phone-free schools, waiting longer before giving children smartphones and social media accounts, and giving children more independence.

Many scientists agree with parts of this, but others say the evidence is weaker than the book suggests. Psychologist Candice Odgers, writing in the science journal Nature, argued that most studies do not find a large, consistent harmful effect. Researchers such as Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski have found that, on average, the links between screen time and well-being in big data sets are real but small. One key problem is that most studies show a correlation, which means two things happen together, rather than proving that one causes the other. If teenagers who feel lonely or depressed tend to spend more time on their phones, is the phone causing the sadness, or is the sadness causing the phone use? It could be both, or something else could be affecting both.

Scientists also point out that phones affect different people differently. For some teenagers, online friends and support groups are a lifeline, especially if they feel alone at school. For others, comparing themselves with filtered, perfect-looking photos, or getting caught up in online arguments, makes them feel much worse. What you do on a phone, and what it replaces, such as sleep, exercise or time with friends, may matter more than the total number of hours.

In 2023 the Surgeon General of the United States, the country's top public health doctor, issued an official advisory saying that there was not yet enough evidence to say social media is safe for young people, and calling for more research and stronger protections. Several countries have since begun limiting social media for younger children. So while scientists continue to argue about how big the effect is, there is wide agreement on some sensible steps: protect sleep, keep up real-world friendships and activities, and notice how different apps make you feel.

Another worry you may have heard is about phone radiation. Phones talk to towers using radio waves, a type of energy much weaker than X-rays, and very different from the kind of radiation that comes from radioactive materials. In May 2011, a group of 31 scientists from 14 countries met in Lyon, France, for the International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization. They classified radio-frequency fields as possibly carcinogenic to humans, which is called Group 2B. That sounds scary, but it is important to understand what it means. Group 2B is used when the evidence is limited, meaning a link has been seen in some studies but chance, errors or other causes cannot be ruled out. The same group includes things like aloe vera extract and traditional Asian pickled vegetables. The chairman of the working group explained that the decision meant there could be some risk, so scientists needed to keep watching. Since then, large studies have not shown that phones cause cancer, and in 2024 the US National Cancer Institute said the evidence so far suggests that phone use does not cause brain or other cancers. Scientists keep studying it, but phone radiation has not been proven to cause cancer.

sections.heading: Eyes Up! Staying Safe on the Road and Online
paragraphs: Some smartphone dangers are much more immediate. One of the clearest is using a phone while driving. Scientists at the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute fitted cameras and sensors in real trucks and watched how drivers behaved. When drivers were texting, they took their eyes off the road for about 4.6 seconds out of every 6 around dangerous moments. At 55 miles per hour, about 90 kilometers per hour, that is like driving the full length of a football field without looking. In the study, truck drivers who were texting were more than 23 times as likely to have a crash or near-crash.

The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration counted 3,308 people killed in crashes involving distracted drivers in 2022, and phones are one of the major distractions. Because of numbers like these, almost every US state, and many countries around the world, have made texting while driving illegal. Many phones now include a driving mode that holds messages until the car stops. If you are a passenger, you can help by offering to read or answer messages for the driver.

Walkers can get into trouble too. People staring at their screens have stepped into traffic, tripped on curbs and walked into poles, fountains and other people. Researchers at the University at Buffalo even suggested that, counting all the little accidents, texting while walking may cause more injuries than texting while driving. Some cities have painted warning signs on sidewalks and added lights at crossings to catch the eye of people looking down. The rule is simple: when you are crossing a street, look up and listen.

Phones can also bring danger to our feelings. Bullying is very old, but cyberbullying, which means bullying through phones, messages, games and social media, has some new and painful features. In the past, a child who was picked on at school could at least escape at home. Now hurtful messages can arrive at any hour. Bullies can hide behind fake accounts, and a cruel post or an embarrassing photo can be shared with hundreds of people in minutes and stay online for a long time.

If it ever happens to you or a friend, experts give clear advice. Do not reply angrily, since that can make things worse. Save the evidence with screenshots. Block the person and report them using the app's reporting tools. Most importantly, tell a trusted adult such as a parent or teacher. Many young people stay silent because they are afraid their phone will be taken away, but adults can help, and nobody deserves to be bullied.

There is one more online danger young people should know about: strangers who pretend to be someone they are not. A person who says they are another 12-year-old gamer might actually be an adult. Safety experts suggest never sharing your full name, address, school or photos with people you have only met online, never agreeing to meet them in person without a parent, and telling an adult right away if anyone makes you feel uncomfortable or asks you to keep secrets. Being careful online is not about being scared. It is about being smart, just as you look both ways before crossing a road.

sections.heading: Who Is Watching? Privacy, Scams and Passwords
paragraphs: Your phone knows a lot about you. It knows where you are, thanks to GPS, Wi-Fi and nearby cell towers. It knows who you talk to, what you search for, which videos you watch and how long you watch them. It may know your face, your fingerprint, your steps and your heartbeat. All of that information is called data, and data is extremely valuable.

Many apps ask for permission to use your location, camera, microphone or contacts. Sometimes that makes sense: a map app needs your location, and a video-call app needs the camera. But some apps ask for far more than they need. In the past, a simple flashlight or game app might quietly collect location data and pass it on to advertising companies. Some firms, called data brokers, buy and combine information from many sources to build detailed profiles of people, which can then be used to target ads. Investigations by journalists have shown that location data that was supposedly anonymous could sometimes be traced back to individual people, revealing where they live and work.

Governments and phone makers have started to respond. Europe's data protection law, known as the GDPR, which took effect in 2018, requires companies to explain what data they collect and gives people rights to see and delete it. In 2021, Apple began requiring apps to ask permission before tracking iPhone users across other companies' apps and websites, and Android has added its own privacy controls. A good habit is to check which apps have permission to use your location and camera, and to switch off anything that does not need it.

Phones are also a favorite target for scammers. You may have seen text messages claiming that a package could not be delivered, that your bank account has been locked or that you have won a prize. These usually contain a link to a fake website designed to steal passwords or payment details. Tricks like this are called phishing, because the scammer is fishing for information, and when they arrive by text message they are sometimes called smishing. Other scammers pretend to be a family member in trouble who urgently needs money, or a company's support team asking you to install an app that lets them control your phone.

The best defenses are simple. Do not tap links in unexpected messages; instead, open the real app or type the website's address yourself. Be suspicious of anyone who rushes you or asks you to keep a secret. Use a different, long password for every important account, which is much easier with a password manager, and turn on two-step verification, so that even if someone steals your password they also need a code from your phone. Newer technology called passkeys lets you sign in with your fingerprint or face instead of a password at all. Finally, install software updates. Updates often fix security holes that criminals have discovered, so an out-of-date phone is like a house with an unlocked window.

sections.heading: Phones Away! The Great School Debate
paragraphs: Picture a classroom where every student has a pocket computer that can play games, stream videos and chat with friends. Now try to teach that class long division. That is the challenge many teachers have described, and it has led to one of the biggest education debates of the smartphone age: should phones be allowed in school?

France was one of the first countries to answer with a nationwide law. In 2018 the French parliament passed a law banning students from using mobile phones in primary schools and middle schools, which in France covers children aged roughly 3 to 15. Students could still bring their phones, but had to keep them switched off and put away during the school day, with exceptions for teaching activities and for students with disabilities. France later went further, testing a digital pause in which middle school students hand their phones in when they arrive.

Many others have followed. In China, the education ministry announced in 2021 that students should not bring phones into classrooms without written permission from their parents. In Australia, the state of Victoria introduced a ban on phones during the school day in its government schools in 2020, and other states followed. The Netherlands began keeping phones out of secondary school classrooms in January 2024. In the United States, Florida passed a law in 2023 banning phone use during class time, and many more states have since adopted their own rules. In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations' education agency, published a major report warning that technology should only be used in classrooms when it clearly helps learning, and it encouraged countries to think carefully about phones in schools.

Supporters of bans say phones distract students even when they are not being used, because a buzz or the temptation to check messages pulls attention away from the lesson. Some studies, including a well-known one from the London School of Economics that looked at schools in English cities, found that test scores improved after schools banned phones, especially for students who had been struggling. Supporters also hope bans reduce cyberbullying during the school day and get children talking and playing together at break time.

Not everyone agrees. Some parents want their children to have phones in case of emergencies, or to arrange how they will get home. Some teachers use phones as learning tools for research, quizzes or photographing science experiments. And researchers point out that the evidence that bans improve mental health is still mixed, partly because schools that introduce bans often change other things at the same time. Many schools have chosen a middle path, such as phones locked in pouches or lockers during lessons but allowed before and after school. Scientists are watching carefully to see which approaches work best.

sections.heading: The Hidden Cost: Mines and Mountains of Waste
paragraphs: A smartphone looks clean and simple, but it contains a remarkable collection of materials dug out of the Earth from all over the world. There is copper in its wiring, gold, silver and palladium in its circuits, tin in the solder that holds parts together, tantalum in tiny electronic components, rare earth elements in its speakers and vibration motor, glass and aluminum in its body, and lithium and cobalt in its battery. Researchers at the University of Plymouth in England estimated that about 15 kilograms of rock and ore must be mined to make the materials for a single phone.

Cobalt shows how complicated this can be. Many lithium-ion batteries use cobalt in their positive electrode, and batteries are now the biggest use of the metal worldwide. According to the United States Geological Survey, about 230,000 tonnes of cobalt were mined in the world in 2023, and about 170,000 tonnes of that, roughly 74 percent, came from one country: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, often shortened to the DRC, in central Africa. Much of the rest came from Indonesia, Russia and Australia, and most of the world's cobalt is then refined in China.

Most of the DRC's cobalt comes from large industrial mines. But a significant share is dug by so-called artisanal miners: men, women and sometimes children who work with hand tools, shovels and sacks, often in dangerous, unsupported tunnels and without protective equipment. Breathing cobalt dust can damage the lungs, and tunnel collapses have killed miners. In 2016, the human rights group Amnesty International published a report describing children working at artisanal cobalt mines and accused major electronics and car companies of not doing enough to check where their cobalt came from. Since then, many companies have promised to trace their supply chains more carefully, and Apple, for example, has said it is moving toward using recycled cobalt in its batteries. Progress is real but incomplete, and human rights groups continue to report problems.

Then there is what happens at the other end of a phone's life. Electronic waste, or e-waste, means any thrown-away item with a plug or battery, from phones and laptops to toasters and televisions. According to the United Nations Global E-waste Monitor published in 2024, the world produced about 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, an increase of 82 percent since 2010. Only about 22 percent of it was properly collected and recycled. The rest was thrown into landfills, stored in drawers or handled informally. If nothing changes, the report predicts about 82 million tonnes a year by 2030.

That waste is a double problem. First, some of it is dangerous. In some places, people recover metals from old electronics by burning cables in open fires or soaking circuit boards in acid, which releases toxic smoke and chemicals that harm workers, children and nearby communities. Places such as the town of Guiyu in southern China became known for this kind of informal recycling. Second, throwing electronics away wastes valuable materials. The Global E-waste Monitor estimated that the metals in 2022's uncollected e-waste were worth about 62 billion US dollars. A tonne of old phones can contain a few hundred grams of gold, far more than a tonne of typical gold ore. Yet recycling currently supplies only about 1 percent of the world's demand for rare earth elements.

sections.heading: Fix It, Don't Toss It
paragraphs: One of the simplest ways to make phones kinder to the planet is to keep each one working for longer. Every extra year a phone is used means one less new phone needs to be mined, manufactured and shipped. But for many years, phones were not designed to be fixed.

Older mobile phones usually had a battery you could pop out with your thumbnail and replace in seconds. As smartphones became thinner and more waterproof, batteries were sealed inside and glued down. Screens were bonded to the frame, and special screws required unusual tools. Some companies began using a practice called parts pairing, in which a phone checks the serial number of a replacement part and may show warnings or turn off features if the part was not approved by the manufacturer. In 2017, iPhone owners discovered that a software update was slowing down some older phones with worn batteries. Apple said this was to stop them from shutting down unexpectedly, apologized for not explaining it clearly and offered cheaper battery replacements.

These frustrations helped grow the right-to-repair movement, which argues that people who buy a product should be able to fix it themselves or take it to any repair shop they choose, with fair access to spare parts, tools and repair manuals. Lawmakers began to listen. New York passed a Digital Fair Repair Act in December 2022, and other US states have passed similar laws. In 2021, Apple announced a self-service repair program that sells genuine parts and tools to customers. The European Union adopted a Right to Repair Directive in 2024 that requires manufacturers to offer repairs at reasonable prices and forbids tricks designed to block repair.

Europe also set new design rules for phones. Since 20 June 2025, smartphones and tablets sold in the European Union must have spare parts available for seven years after a model stops being sold, must receive operating system updates for at least five years, and must have batteries that keep at least 80 percent of their original capacity after 800 full charge cycles. They must also survive drops and resist dust and water, and each model carries a label with a repairability score from A, the easiest to repair, to E, the hardest. A separate EU batteries law, adopted in 2023, will require most portable batteries in devices to be removable and replaceable by ordinary users from 2027, with some exceptions.

Some companies have built their whole business around these ideas. Fairphone, a social enterprise founded in Amsterdam in 2013, designs modular phones that owners can open with a simple screwdriver to replace the battery, screen or camera. It tries to use recycled and fairly mined materials, such as Fairtrade gold, and the repair website iFixit has given most of its phones a perfect 10 out of 10 repairability score.

So what can you do? Use a protective case and screen protector. Keep your phone's software updated. Get a cracked screen or tired battery replaced instead of buying a whole new phone. When a phone really has reached the end of its life, do not throw it in the trash or forget it in a drawer: take it to a proper electronics recycling point or a store take-back program, or pass it on to someone who can use it.

The problems in this part are serious, but they are not hopeless. Scientists are studying how phones affect our minds and bodies more carefully than ever. Designers are adding tools that help us control our screen time. Governments are writing rules about privacy, schools and repair, and engineers are building phones that last longer, use less cobalt and can be fixed with a screwdriver. In Part 19, we will look at what those engineers are dreaming up next.

deepDive: Two of the loudest smartphone debates, about mental health and about radiation, are really debates about evidence, so it helps to know how scientists weigh it. Most research on screens and well-being is correlational: researchers survey thousands of young people about their phone use and their mood, then look for patterns. Large analyses of such data sets, such as those by Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski, have generally found that heavier digital technology use is linked to slightly lower well-being, but that the average link is small, and it shrinks or grows depending on which questions researchers choose to analyze. Correlation leaves the direction of cause unclear: unhappy teenagers may retreat into their phones. To get closer to cause and effect, scientists use experiments, such as asking volunteers to cut back on social media for a few weeks, and natural experiments, such as comparing places where fast internet arrived earlier or later. Some of these find modest benefits from cutting back; others find little change. Supporters of stronger action, such as Jonathan Haidt, argue that the timing of the teen mental health decline around the early 2010s, its appearance in several countries at once, and the experimental results together justify acting now rather than waiting for perfect proof. Critics such as Candice Odgers reply that the evidence is not strong enough and that focusing on phones might distract from other causes. Radiation is a different kind of debate. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies hazards, meaning whether something could cause cancer under some circumstances, not risks, meaning how likely harm is at everyday levels. Its 2011 Group 2B label for radio-frequency fields meant the evidence was limited: some studies of heavy users had seen associations with a brain tumor called glioma, but chance and bias could not be excluded. There is also a physics argument: radio waves do not carry enough energy per photon to break chemical bonds in DNA, unlike X-rays or ultraviolet light, and their main known biological effect is slight heating. Since 2011, brain cancer rates in many countries have not risen in the way they would be expected to if phones were a major cause, even though phone use exploded. That is why health agencies say phones have not been shown to cause cancer, while still supporting further research.
